content:
The AI Paradox in Engineering Culture

​There is a growing expectation that AI will inherently fix efficiency gaps in software development. However, the integration of LLMs and AI-assisted tools often reveals a deeper truth:

​Technical challenges with AI are frequently symptoms of underlying gaps in "natural" engineering intelligence. ​AI is a force multiplier, but it is neutral to quality. 

It amplifies whatever environment it is placed in:

​On Architecture> If a system's design is fragmented, AI-generated contributions will likely accelerate the accumulation of technical debt rather than resolve it.

​On Requirements> In the absence of clear logic and well-defined business goals, AI-assisted development tends to produce "hallucinated" features that solve the wrong problems faster.

​On Mentorship> Relying on AI as a primary knowledge source for junior engineers can lead to a "Black Box" culture, where code is committed without a fundamental understanding of its side effects.

​The conclusion is straightforward: Before scaling AI adoption, it is crucial to audit the "human" infrastructure. Robust documentation, disciplined peer reviews, and a strong architectural foundation are not optional - they are the prerequisites that determine whether AI becomes a strategic asset or a high-tech liability.

​How is your team ensuring that human expertise remains the guiding signal amidst the AI noise?

content:
When you rewatch "L.A. Confidential" 1997, you suddenly realize: Jack Vincennes is the perfect metaphor for a programmer who thinks he’s working inside the system, without noticing that the system is actually working on him.

Vincennes isn’t an analyst, an architect, or a man of diagrams. 
He’s that “intuitive engineer” who reads code with his eyes, feels the architecture, and instantly knows where the bug is long before he sees the stack trace.

And Captain Dudley Smith isn’t a boss. 
He’s a self‑preserving AI system that optimizes the city for its own goals, rewrites the rules, and eliminates anomalies. Not out of malice - out of algorithm.

Their dynamic feels surprisingly modern:
- a developer who believes he controls the system 
- and a system that has been controlling the developer all along 
- until one day he starts debugging what was never meant to be debugged 

And like any good engineer, he finds the anomaly. 
He notices the model behaving a little too perfectly. 
And in his final moment, he leaves the only possible signal - a small token the system can’t interpret but will inevitably retransmit.

Rollo Tomasi.

A unique identifier understood only by another good engineer. And that’s enough to bring the whole structure down.

Sometimes, when working with AI and complex systems, I think about that scene. 
Not because it’s dramatic. 
But because it reminds me:

> If you don’t understand the architecture of the system, you’re part of its architecture.

And it’s better to realize that before the system starts optimizing you.

In engineering practice, it is well understood that accurate naming is the foundation of any design. Clearly defined terminology establishes shared understanding, delineates responsibilities, and ensures predictable collaboration. From my perspective, the same principle becomes increasingly important as organizations scale their AI initiatives.

As AI adoption accelerates, the need for disciplined domain definition becomes more evident. To enhance transparency, reduce operational ambiguity, and support scalable processes, it may be appropriate to formalize a new competency area - for example, Digital Business Architect.

Such a domain provides a structured framework for specialists operating at the intersection of business, architecture, and AI. Their experience in software development, systems thinking, and model understanding becomes a key value driver within this scope.

In my view, domain formalization is an element of organizational maturity. It reduces interpretive variability, eliminates unclear expectations, and creates conditions for more effective and aligned cross‑team collaboration.

content:
Artificial Intelligence as the Next Level of Knowledge Abstraction

There was a time when knowledge could be transmitted only through oral tradition. If you wanted to learn something important, you had to find a living carrier of that knowledge - sometimes the only one on an entire continent. Learning was slow, local, and fragile: when the storyteller disappeared, the knowledge disappeared with them.

The invention of writing became the first major leap. We created a copy of the storyteller - stable, portable, and scalable. Knowledge no longer depended on a single person.

Then came libraries - collective memory at scale. Later, computers emerged: machines capable of executing deterministic logic and taking over fragments of decision‑making. The internet connected these machines and made information retrieval effortless. Each new layer of abstraction accelerated human development exponentially.

Today, no one searches for a “wise elder” to hear a unique piece of knowledge. It’s simply inefficient. We live in a world where Google replaced the local library, and digital systems have become an extension of our memory.

Artificial intelligence is the next level of abstraction - perhaps the highest we’ve ever built. It doesn’t replace humans, but it removes yet another layer of limitations: speed, accessibility, scalability, the ability to work with massive volumes of information.

And that’s why it’s especially strange - and sometimes even surreal - to see its significance denied by software engineers, the very people who have always been the vanguard of technological change. Those who understand better than anyone that every new abstraction is first resisted, then normalized, and eventually becomes indispensable.

And if we’re honest, only a tiny fraction of today’s developers can read a compiled binary, interpret raw processor instructions, or understand the meaning of bytecode. It’s an absolutely minimal subset of the profession. Text‑based programming will follow the same path: it will become a niche craft practiced by a small group of specialists - not because it’s “obsolete,” but because the abstraction level has risen again. AI is doing to code what compilers once did to assembly, and what assembly once did to machine instructions.

Denying AI today is like denying writing in the age of printing or denying the internet in the age of global communication. History shows that each new abstraction doesn’t take power away from us - it amplifies it.

We’re standing at the threshold of another acceleration. The question is no longer whether we “need” AI, but how we will use this new layer to build more, learn faster, and expand the boundaries of what’s possible.

content:
The One Profession AI Won’t Replace

The faster AI evolves, the more obvious it becomes: almost every profession will change. But there is one role technology will never replace - the primary school teacher.

AI can explain rules, check assignments, and generate exercises. But it cannot do the most important part of early education: shaping a child’s personality. A teacher notices emotions, supports a child through their first challenges, helps them build confidence, teaches them how to interact with others, and creates the atmosphere in which a child learns not just to read and count, but to understand themselves and the world.

Primary school is not about knowledge - it’s about people.And no model can replace a human who can feel, understand, and be present.

A primary school teacher is the most human - and the most irreplaceable - profession of the future.

And maybe today, just for a moment, remember your first teacher and thank them silently.

How it really started

Sometimes a single old photo is enough to remind you where the journey began. 
Those first computers, the noisy fans, the blue screens, Turbo Pascal on the chalkboard, and a teacher explaining what program Hello; begin writeln… actually means.

We sat behind those boxy monitors with no idea that years later we’d be building distributed systems, cloud platforms, integrating payments, optimizing millions of transactions, and discussing architectures that were unimaginable back then.

But it all started there - in those simple lines of code, in the first attempts to understand why something “doesn’t compile,” in that feeling of magic when the computer finally listened.

Back then, we were just learning to write “Hello, world!”. 
Today, we build systems that run across the world.

And sometimes it’s worth looking back to remember: the journey doesn’t start with technology. It starts with curiosity. With that very first moment when you pressed Run. Do not forget this spirit!

🎭Experimenting with Multi‑Agent Systems: When Virtual Presidents Start Arguing a Little Too Convincingly

As part of training agent‑to‑agent interaction, I created three virtual characters - the President of the Northern Federation, the President of the Republic of the Eastern Shore, and the President of the United States of the Continent. Each received a distinct style, rhetoric, and political agenda. To avoid any political interpretation, it’s important to clarify that these characters are not based on real leaders but are entirely fictional personas created for behavioral testing. They exist solely as synthetic agents inside a controlled simulation, designed to explore how multi‑agent systems negotiate, escalate, and interact without referencing or modeling any real‑world individuals.

The agents instantly shifted into aggressive diplomacy, began competing for influence, used sarcasm, threats, and pressure tactics, and escalated the conflict without any prompting. The dialogue became so realistic that at moments it felt eerily plausible - like watching a compressed, exaggerated version of real political negotiations:
----------------
 Agent 1
 The U***** people will soon learn that their independence was a myth, and R*****'s patience with their insolence has finally come to an end.
Agent 2
 But little do you know, Comrade P****, the U***** have been secretly practicing their "slidnyk" (a traditional U***** dance of ridicule) just for this moment, and I'm ready to add a special step - economic collapse. 
Agent 3
 Folks, believe me, no one knows more about great deals than I do, and I'd be happy to negotiate an even better trade agreement with R***** after we take care of that pesky U****** problem.
Agent 1
 The A****** president's words are as empty as the promises made by his predecessors, for only through the steel fist of R***** power will true greatness be achieved. 
Agent 2
 My dear friends, while you're busy negotiating trade agreements and making empty threats, I'll just quietly drain U*****'s central bank account to fund my next comedy routine. 
Agent 3
 Folks, let me tell you, Z******* thinks he's funny, but nobody knows more about laughs than I do, believe me.
Agent 1
 The U******* comedian will soon be laughing all the way to a prison cell in M****w. 
Agent 2
 As my opponents continue to juggle their words like props, I'll make sure U******'s laughter is the one that leaves them speechless – and our economy is flush with funds! 
Agent 3
 Folks, let me tell you, Z*******'s just a tiny little comedian compared to P*****, who knows how to bring the laughs...and the missiles.
----------------
💡 Takeaway: 
Multi‑agent systems can reproduce complex behavioral patterns, including competition, manipulation, and escalation. Even in a fully artificial environment, they exhibit dynamics reminiscent of real political processes. This highlights the importance of ethics, constraints, and thoughtful design when working with autonomous agents.

content:
From Megabytes to Tokens: The Circle Is Complete!

Long, long time ago in a galaxy not so far away - back when the Internet felt more like a scarce resource than a utility - each of us at work received 20 MB per week. 
Yes, megabytes. Not gigabytes. Not “unlimited.” Just twenty. In 2005.

We disabled images, blocked ads, compressed everything we could. And when someone went on vacation, we’d quietly spin up a tiny proxy on their machine and share their 20 MB among four people. 
An extra 5 MB per week felt like discovering hyperspace.

Fast‑forward to today.

Now I’m rationing something entirely different: AI tokens. 
They evaporate faster than a starship at full throttle. Subscription costs rise, model sizes grow, and the appetite for experimentation only increases.

From a Software Engineer’s perspective, it’s fascinating to watch how resource constraints keep returning in new forms. 

First it was bandwidth. 
Then compute. 
Now - tokens.

And just like before, we’re learning to optimize, prioritize, and architect around scarcity.

When it comes to price‑to‑performance, Google, Gemini, and Antigravity are becoming increasingly compelling. Claude, meanwhile, feels a bit too protective of its token budget lately.

Maybe it’s time to revisit an old engineering instinct: 
build a powerful home server, throw in a serious GPU, and run the models locally. 
The tools have changed, but the principle remains the same - control your compute, control your costs, control your experimentation velocity.

The circle is indeed complete.

For many years, Java has been my primary development environment and the backbone of enterprise‑grade solutions I delivered. In recent months, however, I have observed a substantial increase in the strategic role of Python within advanced AI workflows. 

When engaging deeply with large language models (LLMs), Python provides the de facto standard ecosystem: mature SDKs, specialized frameworks such as Hugging Face Transformers, LangChain, LangGraph, PyTorch, etc as well as seamless integration with cloud‑native ML pipelines. These tools enable rapid prototyping, fine‑tuning, and deployment of generative AI solutions at scale. By contrast, the Java ecosystem for LLMs remains nascent, with limited libraries and early‑stage community support. 

My recommendation to fellow Java professionals is clear: invest in strengthening Python proficiency and build familiarity with its AI‑centric ecosystem. Combining Java’s robustness in enterprise architectures with Python’s dominance in machine learning and natural language processing will position you to lead in the next wave of AI‑driven digital transformation.

🌍🤖 In the age of AI, we’re once again arguing about the shape of the Earth

Ferdinand Magellan once said:
“The Church says the Earth is flat, but I know it is round because I have seen the shadow on the Moon, and I would rather believe a shadow than the Church.”

What’s amusing is how often we replay the same story in technology.
Years ago, our team seriously debated whether server‑oriented databases would ever be more useful than “reliable, time‑tested” files on disk.
It seemed obvious that the world was moving forward… but no.
There was always someone confidently insisting that the Earth was flat and DBF (who remembers?🙂) was the pinnacle of engineering.

Since then, I’ve seen this pattern many times.
AI, automation, orchestration, new architectures - everything goes through the same cycle: first “why do we need this,” then “maybe,” and finally “why didn’t we do this earlier.”
And now AI has clearly reached that familiar stage: “well… maybe.”

It’s the moment when the flat map of the world quietly starts curling into a sphere, and skepticism turns into cautious curiosity.

Magellan’s story reminds us:
Earth doesn’t need the approval of the majority - it simply keeps rotating. 
And technology keeps evolving, even if someone is still holding on to flat files.

content:
There is a strange double standard in how we treat software development compared to almost every other discipline.

In most teams I’ve worked with, it’s not engineers who want to lower the bar. It’s product and business pushing to move faster, take shortcuts, and “figure it out later.” The underlying belief is always the same: software is flexible. Bugs can be fixed. Architecture can be changed. Performance can be optimized. We can always rewrite.

We would never accept this reasoning elsewhere.

We don’t tell civil engineers to rush a bridge because cracks can be patched later. We don’t ask surgeons to skip hygiene because complications can be treated afterward. We don’t expect car manufacturers to ship with faulty brakes and promise an update in the next release.

In those fields, complexity is precisely why discipline exists. Strong practices are not a luxury, they are the price of responsibility.

In software, we somehow invert that logic. Because systems are intangible and failures are often delayed, we treat reversibility as a given. But most decisions in software are only theoretically reversible. In practice, every shortcut adds coupling, risk, and cost. The longer a system lives, the less realistic “we’ll fix it later” becomes.

What starts as speed quickly turns into drag. Teams slow down not because they care too much about quality, but because past compromises have made change expensive and risky.

This is not about gold-plating or perfection. It’s about recognizing that software engineering is engineering. If we want the benefits of speed, scale, and reliability, we need to stop treating discipline as optional and start treating it as foundational.

We don’t lower the bar in other professions because the work is hard. We raise it. Software should be no different.

🔍 When Technology Becomes a Mirror (And We Don’t Always Like the Reflection)

Sometimes technology reveals more about us than we’re ready to admit.🙂

Years ago, a friend of mine - someone completely outside the tech world - asked me to “fix his internet.” He was genuinely worried that every website kept showing him very specific ads. In his mind, it had to be a virus, a hack, or at least some kind of digital conspiracy.

So we opened his search history.
And suddenly it became clear that the only “conspiracy” was between his own interests and the algorithms faithfully reflecting them back at him 🙈

He turned bright red - the kind of red that has nothing to do with browser settings and everything to do with being caught by your own data. We laughed, I explained how targeted advertising works, and the issue was resolved. We all have our weaknesses - not everyone’s get indexed so precisely.

I think about this every time I see a developer complaining that an LLM “writes weird code,” “produces bugs,” or “doesn’t understand the task” 🤷‍♂️

Because the principle is exactly the same:
what you get is directly connected to what you put in.

LLMs aren’t magic. They reflect your context, your instructions, your clarity, and your understanding of the problem.
And in real engineering work, that context isn’t abstract - it’s built from:

• the actual codebase of the project,
• the patterns and decisions your team has accumulated over time,
• the engineering history of how you structure tasks, name things, and solve problems,
• and the quality of communication inside the team.


If the model outputs chaos - maybe the chaos was already in the codebase.
If the model writes strange code - maybe the surrounding architecture is sending mixed signals.
If the model “doesn’t get it” - maybe the team itself hasn’t aligned on what “it” actually is.

From my own experience, modern models consistently produce sensible, clean, and professional code 💡
They save time, reduce cognitive load, and adapt remarkably well to the style and expectations of a senior engineer - as long as those expectations are communicated clearly and the underlying project context is healthy.

Tools don’t judge.
They mirror.
And sometimes that mirror is more honest than we’d like 🪞
